text: DIRTIER AIR DIRTIER WATER Across wide stretches of the sun-bleached Sonoran desert in Arizona, thousands of retired aircraft sit nose-to-tail in graveyards of metal known as boneyards. ​Many of their engines haven’t been fired up for years. But America’s soaring demand for electricity to power data centers is bringing them back to life. Several companies are racing to strip the engines out of old aircraft to convert them into electrical generators. And data centers, desperate for power, are snapping them up. “They’re getting creative,” said Bill Kleyman, chief executive of Apolo, an A​.I​. platform and infrastructure company. “Just a few years ago, a traditional data center would have been like, ‘Are you kidding me? This is ridiculous.’” Now, data center developers are obsessed with “speed to power,” Mr. Kleyman said. “It’s like, ‘How fast can you get me energy?’” President Trump, aware that the rapid construction of data centers has sparked concerns over rising electricity prices, has pressed center developers to generate their own power. “It was my idea,” he told reporters in August. “Data centers now are mandated by me that they build their own electricity, so they’re not taking it from the grid." A series on the Trump administration’s historic weakening of environmental protections, and the resulting increase in air and water pollution.
